prompt: What ends a statement in Java?
hint: Line breaks mean nothing to the compiler.

choices.text: The end of the line
choices.why: That is Python's rule; `javac` read on past the line end in `Oops.java`.

choices.text: A semicolon
choices.why: Right: and a missing one is reported at the end of the line it belonged to.

choices.text: A closing brace
choices.why: A brace ends a block, which holds several statements; each of those still needs its semicolon.

choices.text: Indentation back to the previous level
choices.why: Indentation is for people; the compiler would accept the whole file on one line.

prompt: `javac Oops.java` printed `Oops.java:4: error: ';' expected` and exited with 1. What is in the directory afterwards?
hint: `ls` was run right after.

choices.text: `Oops.class`, with line 4 left out
choices.why: The compiler never writes part of a class; `ls` showed no class file.

choices.text: `Oops.class`, which fails when `java` reaches line 4
choices.why: Java does not defer a compile error to run time; there is nothing to run.

choices.text: No class file at all, only the two sources
choices.why: Right: one compile error and the file produces nothing.

prompt: The semicolon is missing at the end of line 4. Why does `javac` report it there and not on line 5, where it got confused?
hint: Look at where the caret `^` sits.

choices.text: It points to where it expected the `;`
choices.why: Right: the caret sits after the closing parenthesis, which is where the fix goes.

choices.text: It stops reading at the end of each line and checks it
choices.why: It reads a stream of symbols across lines; that is why it only understood on line 5.

choices.text: Line 5 is fine, so the error must be on line 4
choices.why: The compiler does not reason backwards like that; it names where its expectation failed.

prompt: `system.out.println("Hello, Java");` fails with `package system does not exist`. Why a message about a package?
hint: A lower-case name followed by a dot.

choices.text: `System` is in a package called `system` that Ubuntu does not install
choices.why: `System` is in `java.lang`, always available; nothing is missing from the JDK.

choices.text: A lower-case name before a dot reads as a package, so the compiler looked for one
choices.why: Right: the real mistake is the missing capital, and the message names its consequence.

choices.text: Every name that is not a class is assumed to be a package
choices.why: Only in this position, a name before a dot; a lone unknown name gives `cannot find symbol`.

choices.text: Packages must be imported, and `system` was not
choices.why: Importing would not help; no package `system` exists to import.

prompt: Put the lines of `Hello.java` in order.
hint: Class, method, statement, then the braces close.

prompt: Match each name to what the convention says it is.
hint: Capitals carry the information.

prompt: You copy `Hello.java` to `Greeting.java` and compile the copy. What does the compiler do?
hint: The class inside is still called `Hello`.

choices.text: Compiles it into `Greeting.class`, named after the file
choices.why: Class files are named after classes, and here it refused before writing any.

choices.text: Warns about the convention and compiles it anyway
choices.why: It is an error, not a warning: this is the one naming rule the compiler enforces.

choices.text: Refuses it, naming the file `Hello.java`
choices.why: Right: that is the error, word for word.

prompt: Which name follows the conventions for a method that sends an overdue notice?
hint: A method is a verb, in camelCase.

choices.text: `OverdueNotice`
choices.why: Capitalised and a noun: that is how a class would be named.

choices.text: `sendOverdueNotice`
choices.why: Right: a verb saying what it does, first word lower case.

choices.text: `SEND_OVERDUE_NOTICE`
choices.why: Upper snake case is for constants.

choices.text: `overdue_notice_send`
choices.why: Underscores between words are another language's style, and the verb comes last here.

prompt: Lesson 2's `java Main.java` found `Shout` without being told where it was. Which rule made that possible?
hint: The launcher had only a class name to go on.

choices.text: Class names are PascalCase, so the launcher could tell `Shout` was a class
choices.why: The case convention says what kind of name it is, not which file it is in.

choices.text: A public class lives in a file with exactly its name, so `Shout` could only be in `Shout.java`
choices.why: Right: that is what lets the compiler find a class from its name alone.

choices.text: The launcher compiles every file in the directory and keeps what it needs
choices.why: A broken `Broken.java` beside them was never read, so it does not compile everything.

prompt: Which comment does `javadoc` read?
hint: It has one more character at the start.

choices.text: `//` at the end of a line
choices.why: Line comments are for people only.

choices.text: `/*` … `*/`, which may span as many lines as it needs
choices.why: A block comment is for people; it needs the second star to become documentation.

choices.text: `/**` … `*/` above a declaration
choices.why: Right: placed there, it documents what follows it.

prompt: Which of `Greeter.java`'s comments is the kind the section calls useless, and why?
hint: A comment should say why.

choices.text: The block comment above `END`, because a constant explains itself
choices.why: That one says why the full stop is there, which nobody could tell from `"."`.

choices.text: `// END is defined above`, because it repeats what the code shows
choices.why: Right: and the day `END` moves, it becomes false.

choices.text: The `@param` line, because `javadoc` can read the parameter's name
choices.why: The name is not the meaning; `@param` says what the value is, from the member's card.

prompt: `javadoc -quiet -d docs Greeter.java` printed two warnings. What did they have in common?
hint: `main` was one of them.

choices.text: Both were about tags with a wrong name
choices.why: Both tags in `greet`'s comment were fine; `greet` drew no warning.

choices.text: Both were public and undocumented
choices.why: Right: `main`, and the constructor the compiler wrote for `Greeter`.

choices.text: Both stopped the pages from being written
choices.why: Warnings stop nothing: `docs` held `Greeter.html` afterwards.

prompt: In a documentation comment, the tag that describes what a method gives back is `@___`.
hint: The word for what a method hands back.

prompt: In `jshell`, `int pages = 7 / 2` answers `pages ==> 3`. Why 3?
hint: Both numbers are whole numbers.

choices.text: Dividing one whole number by another gives a whole number
choices.why: Right: the remainder is dropped, and lesson 6 shows why.

choices.text: `jshell` rounds every result for display
choices.why: `pages * 3.0` showed `9.0`; nothing is rounded for display.

choices.text: 3.5 rounded half down to the nearest integer
choices.why: Nothing is rounded: the fraction is cut off, whatever its size, so 19 / 5 gives 3 as well.

prompt: Which of these does `jshell` accept that a `.java` file does not? Choose all that apply.
hint: The section named two.

choices.text: A statement with no semicolon
choices.why: Yes: none of the lines in `try.jsh` ended with one.

choices.text: A statement outside any class
choices.why: Yes: `int pages = 7 / 2` stood on its own.

choices.text: `System` written as `system`
choices.why: Case matters in `jshell` exactly as in a file.

choices.text: Integer division that keeps the fraction
choices.why: `7 / 2` gave 3 there too; it is the same language.

prompt: `javap Hi.class` printed `final class Hi`, and `Hi.java` declares no class. Where did it come from?
hint: Look at the name.

choices.text: From `IO`, which wraps the code it prints
choices.why: `IO` is a separate library class; `Hi` is named after the file.

choices.text: The compiler declared it, named after the file
choices.why: Right: a compact source file still produces a class, implicitly declared.

choices.text: `java Hi.java` wrote it in an earlier run
choices.why: Source-file mode writes nothing to disk; `javac Hi.java` wrote this one.

choices.text: Every class file gets a `final` wrapper class from `javap`
choices.why: `javap` only prints what is in the file; `Hello` printed as `public class Hello`.

prompt: A server has Java 21, and you send it `Hi.java`, a compact source file. What happens when it is compiled there?
hint: `javac --release 21` played the part of that server.

choices.text: It compiles, because compact files are only a different way of writing the same class
choices.why: The class is the same idea, but 21's compiler does not know the syntax.

choices.text: It compiles with a warning, and `IO.println` fails when the program runs
choices.why: It never gets as far as running: the compiler refuses the file.

choices.text: The compiler refuses it: implicitly declared classes need release 25
choices.why: Right: that was the message, with the release to ask for.

prompt: Why does `main` have to be `static`?
hint: What exists when the program starts?

choices.text: So that it can print to `System.out`
choices.why: Any method can print; `static` has nothing to do with output.

choices.text: So the launcher can call it with no object
choices.why: Right: there is no object yet, and lesson 15 explains what `static` means.

choices.text: So that other classes cannot call it
choices.why: That is `private`; `public static` main can be called from anywhere.

prompt: A colleague's file starts `public class reportPrinter` and is saved as `ReportPrinter.java`. What happens, and what should change?
hint: One rule is the compiler's and one is the community's.

choices.text: It compiles, since the names differ only in case
choices.why: Names are case-sensitive, and the file must match the public class exactly.

choices.text: It fails to compile; rename the class `ReportPrinter`, which also follows the convention
choices.why: Right: the file rule is enforced, and PascalCase fixes both at once.

choices.text: It fails to compile; rename the file `reportPrinter.java`
choices.why: That compiles, and leaves a class name every reader takes for a variable.

prompt: In `jshell`, the command that lists every variable with its type is `/___`.
hint: Commands start with a slash.
